sections.heading: What do the symptoms feel like, and how does Parkinson's progress?
sections.body: Parkinson's disease usually develops gradually, and the symptoms are mild at first. The NHS lists three main movement symptoms: tremor, slowed movement and muscle stiffness. The tremor is shaking that typically starts in a hand or arm and is most noticeable when the limb is at rest. Slowed movement is called bradykinesia, and it can lead to a small-stepped, shuffling walk. Stiffness, also called rigidity, can make movement and facial expression harder and sometimes causes painful cramps. Symptoms vary a lot from person to person, and it is unlikely that one person would have all or most of them. The NHS describes the condition as one in which parts of the brain become progressively damaged over many years. Symptoms tend to worsen over time, and everyday tasks can become harder without help.

sections.heading: What other symptoms can happen?
sections.body: Parkinson's also brings symptoms that are not about movement. NHS inform mentions balance problems, a reduced sense of smell, nerve pain, bladder problems, constipation, sweating, swallowing difficulties, and changes in mood or memory. Balance problems can make a fall more likely, and a fall can lead to injury. A loss of the sense of smell sometimes occurs several years before other symptoms develop. Some of these problems can be treated, and swallowing difficulties, for example, may improve with softer food. Depression is common in people with Parkinson's, and dementia can develop later in the disease. A review of advanced disease lists motor fluctuations, involuntary movements, falls, hallucinations and sleep disorders among the complications that can occur.

sections.heading: How is Parkinson's disease diagnosed?
sections.body: The NHS says that no test can conclusively show that someone has Parkinson's disease. A doctor bases the diagnosis on the symptoms, the medical history and a detailed physical examination. During the examination, the GP may ask the person to do simple movement or walking tasks. Early on, symptoms are often mild, so a GP may find it hard to be certain. If Parkinson's is suspected, the GP usually refers the person to a neurologist or a geriatrician, a specialist in problems affecting older people. Blood tests and an MRI brain scan may be ordered to rule out other conditions. A DaT scan is a nuclear imaging test that looks at how dopamine transporters work in the brain. It is often used to help tell Parkinson's apart from other causes of tremor or difficulty with movement, and it is only occasionally needed. For the scan, a tracer is injected into a vein and the person lies still, and the results go to the referring doctor, who arranges a follow-up appointment.

sections.heading: What treatments are used?
sections.body: There is currently no cure for Parkinson's disease, but treatments are available to help reduce the main symptoms and maintain quality of life. The NHS lists medicine, supportive therapies such as physiotherapy and occupational therapy, and surgery for some people. Most people with Parkinson's eventually need a medicine called levodopa. MAO-B inhibitors can also improve symptoms, although their effect is small compared with levodopa. People with severe on-off fluctuations or involuntary movements may be considered for medicine delivered continuously through a tube into the tummy. Deep brain stimulation is a type of surgery that does not cure Parkinson's disease but can ease symptoms for some people. It is usually considered when changes to medicines have not controlled the fluctuations in how well they work. In the early stages people may need little or no treatment, because symptoms are usually mild at first.

sections.heading: Living with Parkinson's disease
sections.body: Regular exercise can help relieve muscle stiffness, lift mood and reduce stress. NHS 111 Wales advises a balanced diet that includes all the food groups. Many people with Parkinson's have problems with speech and swallowing. A speech and language therapist can help with speaking and swallowing exercises. An occupational therapist can pinpoint everyday tasks that are hard, such as dressing or getting to the shops. Physiotherapy and occupational therapy are listed by the NHS among the supportive treatments for Parkinson's. Because balance problems can make falls more likely, the NHS inform page flags falls as a risk to be aware of. Everyday tasks can become harder without help as the condition advances, so practical support from family, carers and health professionals often matters.

sections.heading: What is the outlook?
sections.body: The NHS says that Parkinson's disease does not directly cause people to die, but it can leave them more vulnerable to serious infections. Most people respond to treatment and have only mild to moderate disability. A minority may not respond as well and can, in time, become more severely disabled. NHS 111 Wales says that most people with Parkinson's now have a normal or near-normal life expectancy. One study found that respiratory infection was the leading cause of hospital admission among people with the condition. According to a review of advanced disease, known complications of the condition include falls, motor fluctuations, dementia, hallucinations, sleep disorders and depression. The outlook varies from person to person.

faqs.q: Is there a cure for Parkinson's disease?
faqs.a: There is currently no cure for Parkinson's disease. Treatments are available to help reduce the main symptoms and maintain quality of life, and they include medicine, physiotherapy and occupational therapy. For some people surgery called deep brain stimulation can ease symptoms, although it does not cure the condition.

faqs.q: Can a test confirm Parkinson's disease?
faqs.a: The NHS says that no test can conclusively show that someone has Parkinson's disease. A doctor bases the diagnosis on symptoms, medical history and a detailed examination. Blood tests and an MRI scan may be used to rule out other conditions, and a DaT scan, which looks at dopamine function, may be used in unclear cases.

NHS 111 Wales says that most people with Parkinson's now have a normal or near-normal life expectancy. The NHS says the condition does not directly cause death, but it can leave people more vulnerable to serious infections. A minority of people respond less well to treatment and may become more severely disabled over time.

faqs.q: Does Parkinson's disease only affect movement?
faqs.a: No, because people can also have balance problems, a reduced sense of smell, nerve pain, bladder problems, constipation, sweating, swallowing difficulties, and changes in mood or memory. Symptoms vary a lot, and it is unlikely that one person would have all or most of them. A reduced sense of smell sometimes appears several years before other symptoms.

faqs.q: Who can help with everyday difficulties?
faqs.a: Physiotherapy and occupational therapy are supportive treatments listed by the NHS. An occupational therapist can pinpoint everyday tasks that are hard, such as dressing or getting to the shops. A speech and language therapist can help with speaking and swallowing exercises.

keyFacts.value: Usually develops gradually and is mild at first, with parts of the brain becoming progressively damaged over many years.

keyFacts.label: Who diagnoses it
